content: 1. Intravenous cefotaxime sodium should be administered every 12 hours. It is important to note that antimicrobial treatments are most effective when broad-spectrum, bactericidal antibiotics are initiated after obtaining blood cultures and prior to surgical intervention. For patients with a creatinine clearance (CCr) of ≤20 mL/min, the dose of cefotaxime sodium should be reduced by 50%. 2. Ciprofloxacin should be used cautiously in patients with a CCr ≤50 mL/min or when co-administered with drugs that may alter its metabolism. 3. For patients with a penicillin allergy or MRSA colonization, the preferred regimens include doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily, linezolid 600 mg orally twice daily, or clindamycin 450 mg orally four times daily. However, the benefit and necessity of antimicrobial therapy in early post-implantation inflammation remain unclear. 4. In cases of severe sepsis, the preferred regimen includes vancomycin 1 g intravenously every 12 hours combined with meropenem 1 g intravenously every 8 hours, or daptomycin 8–10 mg/kg intravenously once daily combined with meropenem 1 g intravenously every 8 hours. Gentamicin or other anti-Gram-negative agents may be appropriate depending on local epidemiology. 5. For infections involving ICED-LI, ICED-IE, or generator pocket infections with negative blood cultures, the preferred regimen includes vancomycin 1 g intravenously every 12 hours combined with gentamicin 1 mg/kg intravenously every 12 hours, or daptomycin 8–10 mg/kg intravenously once daily combined with gentamicin 1 mg/kg intravenously every 12 hours. For complicated infections (e.g., endocarditis, septic thrombophlebitis, osteomyelitis, or persistent bloodstream infections despite device removal and appropriate initial antimicrobial therapy), the duration of antimicrobial therapy should be at least 4 to 6 weeks. 6. For methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) catheter-related infections, the preferred regimen includes vancomycin 15 mg/kg intravenously every 12 hours, daptomycin 6–8 mg/kg per day intravenously, or linezolid intravenously. If susceptible, rifampin, gentamicin, or TMP-SMZ may be added. 7. For Enterococcus faecalis or Enterococcus faecium infections that are ampicillin-susceptible, the preferred regimen includes ampicillin 2 g intravenously every 4–6 hours, or ampicillin 1 mg/kg intravenously every 8 hours, or gentamicin 1 mg/kg intravenously every 8 hours. For ampicillin-resistant but vancomycin-susceptible strains, vancomycin 15 mg/kg intravenously every 12 hours ± gentamicin 1 mg/kg intravenously every 8 hours is preferred. For strains resistant to both ampicillin and vancomycin, linezolid 600 mg intravenously every 12 hours or daptomycin 6 mg/kg per day intravenously is recommended. 8. For ESBL-negative infections, ceftriaxone 1–2 g per day intravenously is preferred. Alternatives include ciprofloxacin or aztreonam intravenously. For ESBL-positive infections, ertapenem 1 g per day intravenously, imipenem 500 mg intravenously every 6 hours, meropenem 1 g intravenously every 8 hours, or doripenem 500 mg intravenously every 8 hours is preferred. Alternatives include ciprofloxacin or aztreonam intravenously. 9. For Enterobacter species and Serratia marcescens infections, the preferred regimen includes ertapenem 1 g per day intravenously, imipenem 500 mg intravenously every 6 hours, or meropenem 1 g intravenously every 8 hours. Alternatives include cefepime or ciprofloxacin intravenously. 10. For Acinetobacter infections, the preferred regimen includes ampicillin/sulbactam 3 g intravenously every 6 hours, imipenem 500 mg intravenously every 6 hours, or meropenem 1 g intravenously every 8 hours. 11. For Stenotrophomonas maltophilia infections, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 3–5 mg/kg intravenously every 8 hours is preferred. An alternative regimen includes ticarcillin intravenously combined with clavulanate intravenously. 12. For Burkholderia cepacia infections, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 3–5 mg/kg intravenously every 8 hours, imipenem 500 mg intravenously every 6 hours, or meropenem 1 g intravenously every 8 hours is preferred. 13. For Candida albicans or other Candida species infections, the preferred regimen includes caspofungin (70-mg loading dose, then 50 mg per day), micafungin (100 mg per day), anidulafungin (200-mg loading dose followed by 100 mg per day), or fluconazole (400–600 mg per day). Lipid amphotericin B preparations are an alternative. 14. For Corynebacterium jeikeium (group JK) infections, vancomycin 15 mg/kg intravenously every 12 hours is preferred. Linezolid intravenously is an alternative. 15. For Chryseobacterium (Flavobacterium) infections, levofloxacin 750 mg intravenously once daily is preferred. Alternatives include trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, imipenem, or meropenem intravenously. 16. For Ochrobactrium anthropi infections, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 3–5 mg/kg intravenously every 8 hours or ciprofloxacin 400 mg intravenously every 12 hours is preferred. 17. For Malassezia furfur infections, amphotericin B intravenously is preferred. Voriconazole intravenously is an alternative. 18. For acute mediastinitis secondary to cardiac infection and surgery, the preferred regimen includes clindamycin 450 mg intravenously every 6 hours combined with ceftriaxone 2 g intravenously every 24 hours for at least 2 weeks. 19. For viral myocarditis, supportive care and standard management of congestive heart failure are the mainstays of therapy. Ribavirin and interferon-alpha have shown improved survival in animal models. Temporary pacemaker insertion is indicated for symptomatic bradycardia or heart block during the acute phase. ICD implantation is not indicated during the acute phase but may be beneficial for life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias outside the acute phase. 20. For fungal pericarditis, empiric therapy includes fluconazole, ketoconazole, itraconazole, amphotericin B, liposomal amphotericin B, or amphotericin B lipid complex. 21. For tuberculous pericarditis, the preferred regimen includes isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for 2 months, followed by rifampicin and pyrazinamide for 4 months. Prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg per day is also administered and tapered over 6–8 weeks. 22. For primary prophylaxis of rheumatic fever, penicillin V, amoxicillin, or benzathine penicillin G is preferred. Alternatives include azithromycin, clarithromycin, or sulfadiazine for penicillin-allergic patients. The duration of secondary prophylaxis depends on the presence of carditis and residual heart disease.
